propositions.text: The proceeding involves the 'due care' standard for annual patent maintenance fees introduced in October 2019 under the Patent Act.
The 'due care' standard was introduced to satisfy obligations under the Patent Law Treaty administered by WIPO.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the proceeding concerns the 'due care' standard for patent fees introduced in 2019 to meet Patent Law Treaty obligations.

propositions.text: This is a judicial review of a December 20, 2022 decision of the Commissioner of Patents denying the Applicant's request for reinstatement of Canadian Patent No. 2,690,767.

paragraphs.summary: The court states this is a judicial review of the Commissioner's December 2022 decision denying the Applicant's patent reinstatement request.

propositions.text: The Commissioner was not satisfied the failure to pay the maintenance fee occurred despite due care.
The Commissioner refused to reverse the deemed expiry of the 767 Patent.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found no due care and refused to reverse the patent's deemed expiry.

propositions.text: The Decision was reasonable and there was no breach of procedural fairness.
The application shall be dismissed.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Decision reasonable with no procedural fairness breach and dismisses the application.

propositions.text: Under the Patent Act, annual maintenance fees must be paid to maintain a patent application and issued patent in good standing.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Patent Act requires annual maintenance fees to maintain patent good standing.

propositions.text: If maintenance fees are unpaid by due date, a six-month late fee period applies.
The Commissioner must notify potential deemed expiration if fees remain unpaid after the late fee period.
A patent is deemed expired if fees are unpaid after the late fee period and two months after notice.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains late fee period, notice requirements, and deemed expiration rules under the Patent Act.

propositions.text: A deemed expired patent may be reinstated if subsection 46(5) requirements are met.
Reinstatement requires a request within 12 months, explanation for non-payment, and payment of fees.
The Commissioner must be satisfied the failure occurred despite due care.
The due care requirement arises from Patent Act amendments after Canada joined the PLT.

paragraphs.summary: The court states reinstatement conditions including due care requirement from Patent Act amendments after joining PLT.

propositions.text: Applicant Robert Taillefer and Respondent Sylvain Fredette are named inventors and owners of the 767 Patent.
The 767 Patent is for a wide ice resurfacing machine, described as wider than traditional machines.
Mr. Taillefer allegedly implemented the invention on the Rideau Canal skating surface.
Mr. Taillefer's patent portfolio includes two patents, including the 767 Patent.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the Applicant and Respondent as inventors and owners of the 767 Patent for a wide ice resurfacing machine.

propositions.text: The 767 Patent application was filed January 21, 2010 and issued January 19, 2016.
A patent agency firm was appointed by the Applicant to manage the patent from the outset.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the 767 Patent was filed in 2010, issued in 2016, and managed by an Agent appointed by the Applicant.

propositions.text: From 2012, the Applicant was required to pay annual maintenance fees due about January 20 each year.
The Agent required instructions from Mr. Taillefer before paying the annual maintenance fee.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Applicant had to pay annual fees from 2012 and the Agent needed instructions before payment.

propositions.text: From 2010 to 2019, Mr. Taillefer and the Agent consistently communicated by email using the same address.

paragraphs.summary: The court states consistent email communication occurred between Mr. Taillefer and the Agent from 2010 to 2019.

propositions.text: The Agent sought payment instructions for the 2020 maintenance fee five months early on September 18, 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Agent requested payment instructions for the 2020 fee early in September 2019.

propositions.text: No response was received, so the Agent sent reminders on December 17, 2019, January 6, 2020, and January 20, 2020.
Reminders indicated payment would not be made without specific instructions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Agent sent multiple reminders for payment instructions indicating no payment without instructions.

propositions.text: The Agent did not pay the maintenance fee by January 20, 2020 due to lack of instructions.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Agent did not pay the 2020 maintenance fee by the deadline due to no instructions.

propositions.text: On March 31, 2020, the Agent informed Mr. Taillefer payment was not made and late fee deadline was July 21, 2020.
Two further reminders were sent on July 16 and 17, 2020.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Agent notified Mr. Taillefer of unpaid fees and late fee deadline with further reminders in July 2020.

propositions.text: On October 20, 2020, the Agent notified Mr. Taillefer that the 767 Patent was deemed expired.
On October 29, 2020, Mr. Taillefer found the notice in his junk folder and instructed the Agent to seek reinstatement.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Agent notified expiry in October 2020 and Mr. Taillefer found notice in junk folder and sought reinstatement.

propositions.text: On November 16, 2020, the Agent filed a reinstatement request with fees and explanation about emails found in junk folder.
The Agent stated the Applicant did not cause emails to be junked and acted immediately upon learning of expiry.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Agent filed reinstatement with explanation about junk folder emails and Applicant's immediate action.

propositions.text: On August 3, 2021, the Manager of Patent Policy advised the Agent of intent to refuse reinstatement and invited response.
The Agent submitted a further response on August 31, 2021.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker notified intent to refuse reinstatement in August 2021 and the Agent responded.

propositions.text: On December 20, 2022, the Commissioner refused the Applicant's request to reverse the deemed expiry of the 767 Patent.
The Commissioner was not satisfied the failure to pay fees occurred despite due care as required by paragraph 46(5)(b).

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker refused reinstatement in December 2022, finding no due care as required by law.

propositions.text: The Commissioner found an unexpected communication breakdown between Applicant and Agent.
The Commissioner did not find the Applicant took all measures a reasonably prudent patent holder would to avoid failure.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found communication breakdown but no due care measures taken by the Applicant.

propositions.text: Two broad issues: whether the Decision was reasonable and whether there was a breach of procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The court states two issues: whether the Decision was reasonable and whether there was a breach of procedural fairness.

propositions.text: Reasonableness is the presumptive standard of review of merits: Vavilov at paras 23-25.
Reasonableness is deferential but robust, reflecting legislative intent and judicial restraint: Vavilov at paras 23-25, 75, 83.
Reasonableness review focuses on whether decision is internally coherent and justified by facts and law: Vavilov para 85; Canada Post Corp at paras 2,31.
A reasonable decision bears hallmarks of justification, transparency, and intelligibility: Vavilov paras 91-95, 99-100.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains reasonableness as the deferential standard of review, requiring decisions to be coherent, justified, transparent, and intelligible, citing Vavilov and Canada Post Corp.

propositions.text: Procedural fairness asks if procedure was fair so applicant knew the case and had full chance to respond: Canadian Pacific Railway at paras 54,56.

paragraphs.summary: The court states procedural fairness requires the applicant to know the case and have a full chance to respond, citing Canadian Pacific Railway.

propositions.text: The Commissioner applied a different, higher standard of due care than a reasonable patentee, making the Decision unreasonable and procedurally unfair.
The Commissioner applied illogical and confusing reasoning preventing knowing the case to meet, causing procedural unfairness.
Delay in rendering the Decision was procedurally unfair.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant alleges the Commissioner applied a higher due care standard, used illogical reasoning causing procedural unfairness, and delayed the Decision unfairly.

propositions.text: The Commissioner defined due care as measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take to avoid failure, citing MOPOP section 27.03 and PCT Guidelines paragraph 166M.

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner defined due care as measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take, citing MOPOP and PCT Guidelines.

propositions.text: MOPOP section 27.03.06 requires considering if anything else could reasonably have been done to avoid failure, excluding post-failure measures, considering customary diligence and PCT Guidelines paragraph 166M.

paragraphs.summary: MOPOP section 27.03.06 requires considering reasonable measures to avoid failure, excluding post-failure actions, considering diligence and PCT Guidelines.

propositions.text: PCT Guidelines paragraph 166M(d) guides due care in applicant-agent miscommunication, listing prudent behaviors and communication alternatives.

paragraphs.summary: PCT Guidelines paragraph 166M(d) guides due care in applicant-agent miscommunication, listing prudent behaviors and alternatives.

propositions.text: The Commissioner applied a higher due care standard than MOPOP, citing 'all possible actions' as higher than 'all measures reasonably prudent patentee would take'.
The statement 'all possible actions' must be read in context and does not indicate a higher standard than MOPOP.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Commissioner applied a higher due care standard; the court finds the phrase 'all possible actions' must be read in context and is not higher.

propositions.text: The Commissioner consistently refers to the reasonably prudent patentee standard; 'all possible actions' means 'all measures' in context.
The phrase 'all possible actions, considering circumstances' equals the MOPOP standard of 'all measures' a reasonably prudent patentee would take.

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner consistently applies the reasonably prudent patentee standard; 'all possible actions' equals MOPOP's 'all measures' standard.

propositions.text: The Commissioner mischaracterized the Applicant's argument, implying due care requires reasonable and unreasonable measures, a higher standard.
The court does not find the Applicant's argument persuasive regarding mischaracterization or higher standard.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant alleges mischaracterization implying a higher standard; the court rejects this argument.

propositions.text: The Decision's section is a summary of Applicant's arguments, not the Commissioner's analysis.
The Commissioner consistently applied the MOPOP standard requiring all measures a reasonably prudent patentee would take to avoid failure.
No suggestion the Commissioner sought unreasonable measures; 'all possible actions' does not imply unreasonable measures.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Decision section summarizes Applicant's arguments; the Commissioner applied the MOPOP standard requiring reasonable measures only.

propositions.text: Due care should be found if email system worked reliably and breakdown was unanticipated, per paragraph 166M(d) example; finding otherwise is unreasonable and procedurally unfair.
Neither the unreasonableness nor procedural unfairness arguments based on paragraph 166M(d) example succeed.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues due care should be found if email system worked reliably and breakdown was unanticipated; the court rejects these arguments.

propositions.text: This is not a procedural fairness issue; the Applicant had notice of the due care standard and chance to respond in Preliminary Decision.
The same due care standard was set out in the Preliminary Decision and communicated to the Applicant.
Communication of the standard does not raise procedural fairness issues; any issue is substantive reasonableness review.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no procedural fairness issue as the Applicant had notice and chance to respond; any issue is substantive reasonableness.

propositions.text: Doctrine of legitimate expectations does not apply; paragraph 166M(d) is a non-limiting guideline, not a clear procedural framework or guaranteed result.
Legitimate expectations require clear and unqualified framework: Agraira at paras 94-95; Congrégation des témoins de Jéhovah at para 48.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds legitimate expectations doctrine does not apply as paragraph 166M(d) is a guideline, not a clear procedural framework or guaranteed result.

propositions.text: Paragraph 166M(d) uses 'may' not 'will' regarding due care finding in email failure cases, showing no guarantee of due care.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes paragraph 166M(d) uses 'may' not 'will' for due care in email failure cases, showing no guarantee.

propositions.text: Each case turns on its facts; examples in Guidelines are non-binding and address international priority filings, not maintenance fee communications.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds each case is fact-specific; Guidelines examples are non-binding and relate to priority filings, not maintenance fees.

propositions.text: Applicant's focus on email failure example is too narrow; prudent parties must find alternative communication if usual channels fail.
Technical difficulties do not relieve parties from adopting common sense measures to maintain effective communication for deadlines.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Applicant's focus on email failure example too narrow; the Respondent argues parties must adopt common sense measures despite technical difficulties.

propositions.text: The Commissioner acknowledged Agent's explanation of email failure and efforts to remind Applicant, noting unanticipated junk folder issue.
The Commissioner found Agent's and Applicant's efforts limited and insufficient to meet due care standard in circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner acknowledged email failure explanation and reminders but found efforts insufficient to meet due care standard.

propositions.text: Response focused only on email efforts; no other actions or supporting mechanisms described to ensure effective communication or fee payment.
No information on Applicant's system to monitor fee payment or manage email communication effectiveness.

paragraphs.summary: The Commissioner found no other actions or systems described to ensure effective communication or fee payment beyond email efforts.

propositions.text: Email failure involved a year-long string of reminders critical for fee payment, not a single correspondence failure.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the email failure involved a year-long string of reminders critical for fee payment, not a single failure.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for the Commissioner to expect the Agent to have additional communication mechanisms to avoid communication failure.
It was reasonable to expect alternative measures to ensure the patentee was aware of deadlines after numerous unanswered notices.
There had been a consistent pattern of payment since 2012.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it reasonable for the Commissioner to expect additional communication measures and notes consistent payments since 2012.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for the Commissioner to expect a prudent patentee to ensure their email system was effective if relied upon for fee payments.
The Applicant retained responsibility to instruct the Agent yearly to pay maintenance fees.
The Commissioner reasonably found the Applicant must exercise due care to ensure timely instructions to the Agent via email.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it reasonable for the Commissioner to expect the Applicant to ensure effective email communication and timely instructions to the Agent.

propositions.text: The Applicant disagrees with the Commissioner's consideration of the facts.
Disagreement with the Commissioner’s facts does not constitute a reviewable error.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant disagrees with the Commissioner’s facts, but the court finds disagreement is not a reviewable error.

propositions.text: The Applicant argues the Decision is illogical and confusing.
The issue is one of reasonableness, not procedural fairness.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the Decision is illogical and confusing; the court finds this is a reasonableness issue, not procedural fairness.

propositions.text: There is no confusion in the Decision regarding the standard of due care applied.
The Decision is not inconsistent or contradictory with paragraphs 166K or 166M(a) of the Guidelines.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no confusion or inconsistency in the Decision regarding due care and the Guidelines.

propositions.text: Paragraph 166M(a) of the Guidelines requires a prudent applicant to acquire PCT knowledge or appoint a competent agent.
Paragraph 166K states appointing a qualified agent generally satisfies the due care criterion.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Guidelines paragraphs 166M(a) and 166K on due care and appointing competent agents.

propositions.text: It was reasonable for the Commissioner to find the Applicant must ensure communication with the Agent is working to provide instructions.
Both Agent and Applicant must have mitigation systems to complete the Agent’s role.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Commissioner reasonably required the Applicant to ensure communication systems and mitigation measures with the Agent.

propositions.text: The Respondent notes consistency with International Bureau practice on due care and agent selection obligations.
WIPO’s PCT Working Group document requires applicants to appoint qualified agents and take prudent actions for filings.

paragraphs.summary: The Respondent and WIPO guidelines support the due care expectations for agent selection and applicant actions.

propositions.text: The Commissioner’s highlighting of the Applicant’s failure to describe efforts to pay fees on time is not contradictory to Guidelines paragraphs 166K or 166M(a).
The Applicant was expected to be aware of the yearly maintenance fee and to check email and Agent when notices were not received.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Commissioner’s expectations align with Guidelines and the Applicant’s duty to monitor fees and communications.

propositions.text: The Applicant notes 764 days delay between reinstatement request and Decision issuance, arguing it was unreasonable and prejudicial.
Only one month was provided to respond to the Preliminary Decision, which was unfair.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant argues the 764-day delay and short response time were unreasonable, unfair, and prejudicial.

propositions.text: The Applicant argues risk of third party infringement during delay with no remedy due to safe harbour provision.
There is no evidence of actual third party infringers.

paragraphs.summary: The Applicant alleges risk of infringement during delay; the court finds no evidence of actual infringement.

propositions.text: Blencoe test requires delay to be inordinate and cause significant prejudice to amount to abuse of process.
Prejudice is a question of fact requiring evidence to establish abuse of process from delay.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Blencoe test requiring inordinate delay and prejudice, with evidence needed to prove abuse of process.

propositions.text: The Applicant provided no evidence of direct prejudice from delay, so no abuse of process found.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no abuse of process due to lack of evidence of prejudice from delay.

propositions.text: The application is dismissed for all reasons stated.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for all stated reasons.

propositions.text: No costs are awarded as this is the first judicial review substantively considering due care under subsection 46(5) of the Patent Act.

paragraphs.summary: The court declines to award costs given the novel consideration of due care provisions in this judicial review.
